title: TDDR Rising Narratives — Thursday morning, Nov 19
summary: A snapshot of opposition narratives from the Right and the Far Left as of 7:35 AM ET Thursday, Nov 19, 2026. Built for TDDR (Too Dumb Didn't Read). Sen. Ron Johnson's 'Social Security is a Ponzi scheme' remarks are still the largest query in the set: 6,397 posts in the 24 hours to 7 AM ET (28.84× its prior average), with 2,227 overnight versus 1,077 the night before, even though the topic dropped off the U.S. trends list. Roll Call reports Johnson told his hearing he doesn't 'care' if he pays 'a political price.' On the Far Left, the Jeffries/AIPAC attack cooled from Wednesday's peak (4,395 posts, 3.42×) but found a new clip: Code Pink telling Nancy Pelosi that voters 'wanted something different, not a coronation.' New on the Right: 'Democrats are importing voters,' which combines Rep. Lateefah Simon's Protect Our Neighbors Act, called 'amnesty' because it would let some 10-year-old deportation orders expire, with a Stephen A. Smith clip saying Democrats use immigration to dilute the Black vote (2,208 posts; 2,188 overnight versus 17 the night before). Pressley's reparations-first agenda kept climbing (3,687 posts; 1,887 overnight versus 726), and a Detroit DSA vote to draft AOC for 2028 lifted the DSA card (1,477 posts, 1.99×). Fraud claims about Iowa and Texas rose overnight while Texas began a routine risk-limiting audit. Three faded cards were dropped: Arizona ballot harvesting, 'AOC is an actor' and USAID.

trends.detail: U.S. trends were pulled at about 7:11 AM ET with x.get_trends_by_woeid (WOEID 23424977, max 50; 50 returned). Video games (GTA 6, GTA VI, Vice City, Red Dead), morning greetings and the NBA dominated. None of the political names matched a scored query, so no card received the trend bonus this morning. 'Social Security,' 'Ponzi' and 'Ron Johnson,' on the list last evening, were gone. 'Tillis' matches an X News story on Sen. Thom Tillis blocking Sen. Rick Scott's lifetime lobbying ban for former lawmakers; we did not score it. 'Xi Jinping,' 'Vladimir Putin' and 'APEC' reflect foreign news. An X News search for 'Dark MAGA' returned no U.S. story about the phrase, so we did not research it further, and we did not research 'Delcy.' We requested tweet_count, but the trend objects did not include it, so trend volumes are unavailable and we did not estimate them.

oppositionNote.body: Right = narratives the Right is pushing after the Democratic midterm wave. Far Left = pressure on Democratic leadership and the incoming majority from the party's left. This morning the Jeffries fight is still the left's main target, with Code Pink now aiming at Pelosi as well. The Social Security card stays tagged Right because the 'Ponzi scheme' frame is a Right talking point, even though most of the posts matching it are Democratic backlash. The new immigration card is tagged Right: Stephen A. Smith is a registered independent, but the 'importing voters' and 'amnesty' frames are the Right's. The tag is the primary opposition frame.

methodology: Last updated Thursday, Nov 19, 2026, 7:35 AM ET. This is a research snapshot for TDDR, not a live API. U.S. X trends were pulled at about 7:11 AM ET. Last evening's snapshot (Nov 18, 5:45 PM ET) is kept in the archive and was not overwritten. All seventeen of its narratives were re-counted with the same queries so momentum compares like with like. The new 24-hour window overlaps last evening's by 10 hours (7 AM to 5 PM ET Wednesday), so we also report each query's 5 PM–7 AM ET overnight count against the same hours a night earlier. Three narratives were dropped because they faded: Arizona ballot harvesting (86 posts in the last 24 hours; 7 overnight versus 236 a night earlier), 'AOC is an actor' (567 posts, 0.18×), and 'Democrats want to bring back USAID' (640 posts, 0.23×). One was added with a new query: 'Democrats are importing voters' (the Protect Our Neighbors Act and Stephen A. Smith's remarks). Other candidates were counted and not carved out as cards: Code Pink's confrontations with Pelosi and Ocasio-Cortez (807 posts, 4.11×; 727 overnight versus 105), folded into the Jeffries/AIPAC card; Iowa and Texas fraud claims (1,836 posts, 0.74×), which overlap the rigged-midterms card; a Salzburg 'resistance summit' / 'color revolution' query (178 posts, 1.10×); and a Hasan Piker / Neera Tanden 'margin too big' query (314 posts, 0.55×).

For each narrative we ran one English-language X search with x.get_posts_counts_recent at hourly granularity over a 167-hour window from 8:00 AM ET Thursday, Nov 12 (the earliest whole-hour start the recent-count API allowed at pull time), through 7:00 AM ET Thursday, Nov 19. The last 24 hourly buckets (7:00 AM ET Wednesday, Nov 18, through 7:00 AM ET Thursday, Nov 19, exactly 24 hours) give the 24-hour count, and the whole window gives the 'seven-day' total. We counted named news or fact-check outlets whose coverage we opened or retrieved in this morning's searches and cite on the card. Official government pages, bill text, advocacy groups, research groups, pollsters, bill trackers, blogs, X News summaries, and X posts are cited as sources but not counted as outlets. We re-researched the Social Security, Jeffries/AIPAC, reparations and rigged-midterms cards, plus the new immigration card, and counted only outlets retrieved this morning on those cards, which is why some outlet counts changed. We pulled a fresh post sample for the DSA card but no new coverage, so its outlet count is carried over. For the other cards, which we did not re-research this morning, the outlet count is carried over from last evening, and each of those cards says so. We noted whether each topic appeared on the U.S. trends list at about 7:11 AM ET.

Score = 50% volume index + 30% acceleration index + 20% coverage index. Volume index is 100 × log10(1 + last-24h posts) / log10(1 + the highest last-24h count in this set). Acceleration index is 100 × min(last-24h / prior daily average, 3) / 3, so a triple-or-higher average scores 100. Prior daily average is (seven-day total − last 24h) / 6. Coverage index is 70 × min(outlets, 7) / 7, plus 30 if the topic was on the U.S. X trends list this morning. No card got the trend bonus this morning, so scores fell compared with last evening for cards that had it. The Social Security query had a low baseline before Wednesday, so its acceleration index is maxed out. Read the post counts alongside the scores. Evening-to-morning score changes also reflect the lower volume ceiling (6,397 this morning versus 7,753 last evening) and how much coverage we retrieved.

Counts are query matches, not unique posts or unique users, and queries can overlap. The Jeffries/AIPAC, Jeffries Iran funding, Jeffries ATM and DSA queries share many speaker-race posts. The Social Security query also catches posts attacking Johnson, which were most of last evening's sample. The new immigration query includes the phrase 'Stephen A' with any of Democrats/immigration terms, so it can catch unrelated Stephen A. Smith posts that mention Democrats; a narrower count of only the bill found 281 posts. The shutdown query needs both 'shutdown' and an Iran/Medicaid/deadline term, and the rigged-midterms query also catches posts mocking fraud claims. Replies are included, and automated @grok replies make up a visible share of several queries. Sentiment is a qualitative label from relevancy-sorted post samples and from quotes in news coverage, not a scientific poll. This morning we pulled fresh samples for the Social Security, Jeffries/AIPAC (Code Pink), reparations, DSA, rigged-midterms and immigration queries. Other cards carry last evening's sentiment and say so. Daily bar charts use UTC days (a UTC day starts at 7:00 PM ET the previous evening). Bars marked * are partial windows. Hourly charts are labeled in ET.

disinfo.caveatLead: A fact-check is not a volume score.
disinfo.caveatBody: New this morning: 'The Protect Our Neighbors Act wipes out 1.6 million deportation orders' is misleading: 1.6 million is the total number of final orders, but the bill covers only orders at least 10 years old for people with no criminal conviction, and a judge can renew one. 'Democrats are importing voters' runs into the law: green-card holders and other noncitizens cannot vote in federal elections, and PolitiFact rated a related Trump claim Pants on Fire. Posts saying Iowa and Texas results prove fraud have no evidence behind them; Texas's new risk-limiting audit is a routine check required by 2021 state law. Code Pink's point that Jeffries took AIPAC money is accurate (Snopes); claims that pro-Israel members delivered his 251-11 win remain guesses, since the ballot was secret. Carried over from last evening: 'Social Security is a Ponzi scheme' is a comparison PolitiFact has rated False when others made it, and Johnson himself called his 'shut it down' line 'imprecise'; 'Pressley's H.R. 40 pays reparations' is misleading, since it creates a study commission and no vote is scheduled; 'Jeffries backs the Iran war' is false as stated; the '1.2 million signatures' figure against Jeffries remains unverified; there is still no evidence this week's outages were a cyberattack; 'Democrats will defund the military to shut down the government' is misleading; and Lead Stories found no '30,000-case' Texas voter fraud probe.

The most-engaged posts in the sample attacked him ('Social Security is sacrosanct,' 86 likes) or noted he has used the line since 2010 and opposes taxing income above $184,500. The Right's version circulated through RealClearPolitics ('Young People Should Be Furious') and @LeadingReport's 'legal Ponzi scheme' post, the most-liked post we saw. New reporting this morning: Roll Call says Johnson told the hearing that if he has 'to pay a political price for that, I really don't care,' and notes the Social Security trustees project a 22% benefit cut by the end of 2032 without a fix. WPR reports Johnson's chairman's memo was titled 'Social Security: The Reality… a Legal Ponzi Scheme' and that nearly 1.4 million Wisconsinites get benefits. Newsweek quotes Maya MacGuineas of the Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget: 'It is not a Ponzi scheme.' Spectrum News says Johnson projects a $511 billion Social Security shortfall in 2032. Last evening's card (5:45 PM ET): New this evening, and on the U.S. trends list ('Social Security,' 'Ponzi' and 'Ron Johnson' all appeared at about 5:12 PM ET). The busiest hour was 12 PM Wednesday (569 posts). On Fox Business Wednesday morning, Sen. Ron Johnson (R-Wis.), the Senate Budget Committee chairman, said: 'At this point, there's really no way to fix Social Security. It's a Ponzi scheme. You can't fix it, you just shut it down and hope that you can recover some of your money' (The Hill, HuffPost, MarketWatch). He made a similar case on Newsmax, citing the SEC's definition of a Ponzi scheme (MS NOW). At his hearing, 'Social Security: The Reality,' Sen. Ron Wyden said it was the first time in decades a senior senator said he would rather shut the program down than fix it; Johnson answered that his statement was 'imprecise' and that he is 'not proposing shutting down Social Security' (The Hill). An X News summary says a Johnson committee report projects trust-fund depletion by 2032 and calls the program a 'legal Ponzi scheme.' MarketWatch cites the CBO: if the trust funds run out, benefits could fall about 26%. This is a Right narrative that mostly spread as a Democratic attack; we score it because the 'Ponzi' frame itself is moving, and because it previews the 2027 fight over the payroll tax cap.
talkingPoints: Social Security is a Ponzi scheme: today's workers pay today's retirees.
Young people will never see a dime of what they paid in.
It's not your money — Congress already spent it.
It's going broke by 2032 and nobody in Washington will say so.
Let workers invest in the market instead.
narratives.amplifiers: Right: @SenRonJohnson (Fox Business, Newsmax, and his hearing memo); reposts of Fox News's 'legal Ponzi scheme' headline by small accounts such as @MagaWarrior_USA and @TRUMPGIRL_STL. Backlash: Democratic Sens. Ron Wyden and Jeff Merkley at the hearing (Roll Call, Spectrum News), the Alliance for Retired Americans (WPR), and accounts such as @BythePeople18.
narratives.whyItWorks: 'Ponzi scheme' is a sticky, intuitive metaphor for a pay-as-you-go system, and genuine insolvency projections give it a factual hook. It speaks to young workers' fear that they pay in and get nothing, and it moves the debate from 'how to fix' to 'whether to keep.' For Democrats, the 'shut it down' quote is a gift, which is why the backlash outran the original.
narratives.audience: Libertarian and fiscal-conservative voters, younger right-leaning men skeptical of entitlements, and Fox Business/Newsmax audiences. The backlash reaches seniors, Wisconsin voters and the broad Democratic base.
narratives.counter: Use his own walk-back: even Johnson now says he isn't proposing to shut it down. Then explain the difference: a Ponzi scheme is a fraud that hides how it works; Social Security is a public, legally mandated program that can be kept solvent by changing taxes or benefits (PolitiFact). Name the fix: lifting the payroll tax cap ($184,500 in 2026, per The Hill) closes much of the gap without cutting benefits.

factChecks.claim: Social Security is a Ponzi scheme.
factChecks.detail: PolitiFact rated Rick Perry's Ponzi comparison False in 2011 and, reviewing the same claim from Elon Musk in 2025, said that unlike a Ponzi scheme Social Security is transparent, has oversight, promises no unrealistic returns, and can be made solvent through changes to taxes or benefits. It also noted the superficial similarity: current workers' taxes pay current retirees. PolitiFact has not rated Johnson's Nov. 18 remark.

factChecks.detail: On Fox Business he said 'you just shut it down.' From 5 PM ET Wednesday to 7 AM ET Thursday the query matched 1,612 posts, versus 3,506 in the same hours a night earlier. The query cooled from last evening's peak but is still 3.42 times its prior daily average. Overnight it was driven by video of Code Pink activists confronting Nancy Pelosi after Wednesday's 251-11 vote: asked what she would tell people who voted for change, Pelosi said 'They're getting change'; the activist answered that Jeffries 'supported AIPAC and got money from AIPAC… we wanted something different, not a coronation' (@TheTNHoller's clip: 1,780 likes, 35,565 views). Code Pink co-founder Medea Benjamin also pressed Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez on why she backed Jeffries (TRT World). A separate count of Code Pink + Pelosi/Jeffries/AIPAC/'coronation' posts found 807 in the last 24 hours (4.11×), 727 of them overnight versus 105 a night earlier; we folded it into this card rather than scoring it separately. The Washington Post and Common Dreams report that at least seven progressives voted no, citing unresolved commitments on Medicare for All, ICE, corporate money and Gaza. Snopes found Jeffries has received AIPAC money; OpenSecrets estimates about $1.74 million from pro-Israel donors through 2024. Last evening's card (5:45 PM ET): Evening update (Nov 18): 6,296 posts in the last 24 hours, 7.67 times the prior daily average (this morning: 3,675 and 3.68×). From 7 AM to 5 PM ET Wednesday the query matched 2,787 posts, versus 162 in the same hours Tuesday. The query's busiest day of the week: it more than tripled the 7 AM–5 PM count of any other day in the window. House Democrats nominated Jeffries for speaker Wednesday morning by a closed-door, secret-ballot vote of 251-11 (AP, NBC News, NPR, Reuters). No one ran against him. Seven of the 11 'no' votes, all incoming progressives (Reps.-elect Darializa Avila Chevalier, Adam Hamawy, Frederick Haynes, Melat Kiros, Donavan McKinney, Chris Rabb and Claire Valdez), said in a joint statement that on 'Medicare for All, stopping ICE terror, getting money out of politics, or ending the genocide in Gaza' there is 'still work to be done' and that talks with Jeffries are ongoing (NBC News). He needs 218 votes on the House floor on Jan. 3; NBC projects Democrats will hold 259 seats, so he can lose about 40. Online, the loss did not cool the AIPAC attack. Posts recirculated his pro-Israel PAC totals and old AIPAC speeches, and an X News summary of the vote repeated the '1.2 million signatures' petition figure, which we still could not verify. X News also clustered a CODEPINK video of activists pressing Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez on why no progressive challenged Jeffries, and a fight over Mehdi Hasan calling him one of the Hill's worst speakers. His refusal to back defunding the Iran war, a separate thread, has its own card this evening.
talkingPoints: 251-11 is what AIPAC money buys.
He calls Jerusalem New York's 'sixth borough' and wants to be your speaker.
The 11 'no' votes are the only Democrats who listened to voters.
1.2 million people signed to replace him and the caucus ignored them.
Unity means falling in line behind the donors.
narratives.amplifiers: Left: @codepink and co-founder Medea Benjamin; @TheTNHoller's clip (1,780 likes, 35,565 views); @trtworld; Common Dreams. Pushback: commentators cited by X News, including Shermichael Singleton and Paul Begala, who called some nicknames racist; Daily Kos argued the 'haters are mainly online.'
narratives.whyItWorks: A lopsided, secret-ballot vote is easy to read as insiders protecting their own, and the AIPAC money gives the left a single, concrete villain for every disappointment, from Gaza to Iran to Medicare for All. The 11 named no votes make the resistance look real and organized, and the petition number makes it feel like the base was overruled.
narratives.audience: Progressive and pro-Palestinian activists, DSA and Justice Democrats networks, young left voters who drove the midterm wave, and left media audiences (CODEPINK, Truthout, Breaking Points-style shows). The Right reshares it as a 'Democratic civil war.'
narratives.counter: Lead with the incoming progressives' own words: they say talks with Jeffries are producing 'meaningful progress' and are ongoing. Point to concrete wins (AOC leading the healthcare working group, a promised early war-powers vote) and separate verified money figures from inflated ones: OpenSecrets data show far less from AIPAC itself than the viral totals. Don't call critics racist by default; argue the record.

Lateefah Simon (D-Calif.) is introducing the Protect Our Neighbors Act on Thursday: final removal orders would expire after 10 years for people continuously present in the U.S. with no criminal conviction, and those people could seek a green card. A judge could renew an order on 'clear and convincing evidence' (ABC News). Former acting ICE Director Todd Lyons told lawmakers there are about 1.6 million people with final orders, but not all would qualify, and ABC says the bill is unlikely to move before January. Second, X News summarized a barbershop conversation in which Stephen A. Smith, now registered independent, argued that Democrats' immigration policies build a Latino voting bloc and reduce reliance on Black voters, a point he has made before on SiriusXM (Yahoo Sports quoted him calling open borders 'a direct assault against Black voters'). Roland Martin called the argument nonsensical, per X News. An earlier spike on Nov. 13 (5,100 posts that UTC day) came from coverage of President Trump's interview with Smith, in which Trump said immigration reform is 'possible' (USA Today); that spike raises the prior daily average, which is why acceleration is only 1.88×. A narrower count of only the bill (its name, Rep. Simon, or 'deportation orders expire') found 281 posts, 274 of them overnight, so most of this query's volume came from the Smith clip.

At The Atlantic Summit on Tuesday, Jeffries said Democrats will 'move aggressively to end the reckless and costly war of choice in Iran right out of the gate' and pass a war powers resolution in the first week of the new Congress (Jewish Insider). Asked by Jeffrey Goldberg whether ending the war means not funding operations in the Gulf, he answered, 'Well, no. It means a cessation of hostilities' (Truthout). He also said party appropriators are 'in active conversation' about either a funding deal before Dec. 11 or a continuing resolution 'into some point next year' (Common Dreams, citing Punchbowl). Anti-war groups and progressives read that as a refusal to use the Dec. 11 deadline to cut off war money, which Sen. Chris Van Hollen and others have pushed; Just Foreign Policy called it 'a huge betrayal of voters' (Common Dreams). The backlash hit as he won the speaker nomination Wednesday. Common Dreams cites a Reuters/Ipsos poll finding 71% of Americans favor legislation to end the war. In a NPR interview Nov. 6, Jeffries had said Democrats 'shouldn't have to wait' for the new Congress to act. This is the mirror image of the Right's 'Democrats want a third shutdown' card: the same deadline, attacked from the other side.
talkingPoints: Democrats won on ending the war — and Jeffries won't use the one lever that ends it.
A war powers resolution is a press release Trump will veto.
Every week of a continuing resolution is another week of war funding.
He's putting AIPAC first, again.

narratives.whyItWorks: It turns the party's winning midterm message, ending an unpopular war, into a test Jeffries appears to fail on his first day as nominee. 'Defund it' is simple and concrete, while a war powers resolution sounds procedural and veto-able. It also links neatly to the AIPAC frame, so one story feeds the other.
narratives.audience: Anti-war progressives, Van Hollen and Khanna supporters, DSA and left media audiences, and some moderate Democrats who want leverage used before January.
narratives.counter: Be precise about what he said: he committed to a war powers vote in week one and is negotiating the Dec. 11 package; he has not voted to fund the war. Then answer the leverage question directly: if the plan is a short continuing resolution, say how long and what happens if Trump vetoes the war powers resolution. Vague process answers feed the 'caving' frame.

In Iowa, a candidate winning more votes than her party's registered voters is ordinary when independents and crossover voters back her. This is TDDR's read of that reporting, not a rating from a fact-check outlet.

factChecks.claim: Texas just opened a major investigation into 30,000 cases of voter fraud after the midterms.

talkingPoints: The left can't handle free speech — they shouted down a Border Patrol hero.
You have every right to protest. You have no right to shut down a speaker.
A Democratic governor attacked students for inviting a conservative.
He came back and finished the speech. They lost.
This is what the new Democratic majority looks like on campus.
narratives.amplifiers: @EricLDaugh (Turley clip: 2,904 likes, 1,165 reposts, 61,962 views); @DKH013 ('Leftists just WENT BERSERK,' 5,883 views); @NathanielSami and @LegInsurrection on Sherrill's statement. Morning amplifiers: @RyanAFournier (2,087 likes, 613 reposts, 40,280 views); @Ravious101 (243 likes, 7,475 views); @EricLDaugh (footage, per quoting posts); @iDenville; @defnoodlesreal; @MDBayNews and @NathanielSami on Sherrill's statement.
narratives.whyItWorks: Campus shout-downs are a reliable Right-wing story because the video does the work: a calm speaker, a screaming crowd, police in between. It also pins the disruption on the new Democratic governor and recasts an immigration fight as a free-speech fight, where the Right is more comfortable.
narratives.audience: Conservatives, free-speech and anti-'woke campus' voters, parents of college students, and immigration hawks.
narratives.counter: Separate the two things. The governor criticized the invitation and promised to protect the event, and it went ahead. Shouting down a speaker is a bad look and a gift to him; say so. Then bring it back to the record people were protesting: two Americans killed in Minneapolis on his watch.

factChecks.claim: Gov. Mikie Sherrill tried to stop Greg Bovino from speaking at Rutgers.
factChecks.detail: Sherrill condemned the Rutgers Republicans' invitation and urged students to challenge Bovino, but said the state would work with Rutgers to protect public safety and constitutional rights. Rutgers said the club was permitted to host him, and the event went ahead after a roughly 10-minute interruption. This is TDDR's read of NJ.com and CBS New York reporting, not a rating from a fact-check outlet.

talkingPoints: Make America Nice Again — says the party that wants to jail Trump's staff.
'Nice' is a slogan, not a policy.
They called us fascists for ten years. Now they want to be nice?
Democrats can't decide whether to be nice or 'choke them out.'
narratives.amplifiers: Named accounts in posts we opened: @RoyalSerf (5,779 likes, 156 reposts, 94,541 views, plus follow-ups at 7,144 and 3,860 views); @MountainMan280 replying to Axios (73 likes, 1,788 views); and 'JUST IN' copies from @NathanielSami and @JOHNBAXTER_CEO. X News clustered the reaction twice.
narratives.whyItWorks: A soft slogan is easy to mock, and it invites the Right to collect examples of Democrats behaving badly. It also exposes a real split inside the party — fighters versus uniters — that the Right can work from either side.
narratives.audience: Online conservatives and meme accounts, plus left-leaning 'fighter' Democrats who dislike the 'be nice' framing.
narratives.counter: Point out that this is an Axios trend piece about a debate, not a slogan any candidate is running on. Then turn it around: the winners Axios cites won red states by talking about neighbors and decency. If the Right wants to argue against decency, let it.
